newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Labour row rocks trade meet, progress on infotech.
newsitem.headline: Labour row rocks trade meet, progress on infotech.

text.p: Intense haggling among the world's trade ministers brought within grasp on Tuesday a lucrative deal to free the global information technology market.
But a fierce row over labour standards pitted the United States against much of the developing world on the second day of the inaugural ministerial meeting of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).

Big powers, notably the United States and the European Union (EU), said a flurry of closed-door talks had inched toward a global pact to eliminate tariffs on a $600 billion market for items such as computers and microchips.
Storm-clouds over whether to discuss monopolistic business practices also began to disperse. Differences over "new issues" such as agriculture and corruption in trade were narrowing too.
But deadlock surfaced on whether the final conference declaration that would point the way toward free trade in the 21st century should refer to ending labour rights abuse.

Several diplomats emerging from the negotiations said the United States had taken a tough stand on its demand, which many developing nations fear is being used as a means of eroding the developing world's commercial advantage of cheap labour.

Washington had indicated that unless it won mention of the labour issue in the final declaration it would not accept several other parts of the document -- repeating a threat it had already made in Geneva that it would block a declaration to be adopted on Friday unless it got its way, the envoys said.
But WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero told Reuters that he was pleased with the level of progress on an issue that has emerged as the most divisive at the Singapore meeting.
"We are making good progress, I am very encouraged," he said.
"It's going a lot better than I expected," he said, adding that one Asian country that had been taking a very strong line had "made a very useful proposal". Envoys identified the country as Malaysia.
"This has been the most difficult issue and that was evident tonight," WTO spokesman Keith Rockwell told reporters.
The depth of divisions was underlined when Ruggiero moved to calm the debate by asking delegates if they wanted "this ship to sink" -- a reference to the world trading system, envoys said.
Progress was clearer on removing infotech tariffs.

The EU, along with the United States, Canada and Japan, were inching toward consensus on an Information Technology Agreement (ITA) that would be the crowning achievement of the meeting, EU Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told reporters.
"We are making a lot of progress," Brittan said after a lunchtime meeting of the four major trading partners to discuss types of products to be covered and timing of tariff reductions.
Acting U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefksy said she concurred with his comments, but declined to say anything more on the proposed pact to remove tariffs on computer products by 2000.

"There is no question that what the industrialised countries now hope for most here is a deal on information technology products and agreement to work hard for a basic telecommunications pact by February," said one key negotiator.

Signals from negotiators left little doubt the major traders were aiming for agreement as quickly as possible -- perhaps by Wednesday -- to convince Asian trading partners to sign on to the agreement by the end of the meeting on Friday.
Several Asian nations voiced reservations, with Malaysia saying the goal of free commerce in infotech by the turn of the century was too ambitious.

The 128 full delegations from WTO member countries and ministers and officials from nearly 30 others waiting to be admitted heard ringing appeals for progress to a telecoms liberalisation pact with a deadline set for mid-February.
Aiming to counter lobbying by sceptical Western-based aid groups, the WTO insisted that the poorest nations stood to reap major benefit from the freeing of global commerce.

But WTO officials admitted that Ruggiero had failed to convince richer members, both industrialised and emerging economies, to remove all tariffs and other barriers affecting goods from the laggard states.
The EU made little headway in efforts to persuade its main trading partners to jump-start stalled talks on China's bid for WTO admission.
But Russia, another major member-in-waiting, expected to win entry by the end of 1997, Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Oleg Davydov said.
